title: Global Trade Outlook and Statistics, March 2026 (Middle East conflict weighs further on slowing trade outlook)
key_claim: World merchandise trade volume grew 4.6% in 2025 and is forecast to slow to a still-positive 1.9% in 2026 in the baseline scenario, normalising after a surge in AI-related products and the frontloading of imports ahead of tariffs; 2.6% growth projected for 2027. Trade is resilient rather than retreating.
notes: Tier 1 multilateral primary data and forecast. Release date 19 March 2026 confirmed via WebSearch (WTO news item stat_19mar26 and corroborating coverage); paired publication gtos0326.

title: World Economic Outlook, April 2026: Global Economy in the Shadow of War
key_claim: Trade is being rerouted through new partners and regional agreements that do not necessarily align with old geopolitical boundaries; as cross-border flows are rerouted via 'connector' countries, the less effective the policies driving fragmentation may be in achieving their stated objectives. Global growth projected at 3.1% in 2026.
notes: Tier 1 multilateral flagship. Published 14 April 2026 (Spring Meetings). Existence and rerouting/connector-country content confirmed via WebSearch (IMF WEO page, Chapter 1 PDF, IMF blog 14/04/2026).

title: Global Trade Update (April 2026): Global trade growth continues, but fragility rises
key_claim: Goods trade grew about 7% in 2025 (adding roughly $1.8 trillion) and services about 8%; South-South trade expanded about 9%. US-China trade contracted sharply, falling roughly a quarter (about $170 billion) in 2025, while 'connector economies' such as Cambodia, Egypt, Vietnam and Indonesia emerged as intermediaries stabilising trade flows.
notes: Tier 1 multilateral primary data (UNCTAD/DITC/INF/2026/4). Published early April 2026; announcement date ~7 April 2026 confirmed via WebSearch. Direct WebFetch of the publication and news pages returned JS shells; figures corroborated across multiple search results.

title: Fragmenting world worsens finance squeeze, reversing decades of progress on development (Financing for Sustainable Development Report 2026)
key_claim: Average tariffs on least-developed-country exports surged from 9% to 28% in 2025; for developing countries excluding China, average tariffs increased more than eightfold, from 2% to 19%. FDI fell 11% in 2024 to $1.5 trillion. The report concludes that economic hyper-globalization is no longer viable and recommends a multilayered approach to international cooperation; the value of South-South trade rose more than fourfold over 20 years.
notes: Tier 1 UN inter-agency report. UN news announcement of FSDR 2026, dated 9 April 2026. WebFetch verified, full content retrieved.

title: Internal Value Chains Remain Dependent on China Even as Multinationals Shift Production to America
key_claim: China-plus-one strategies have increased geographic diversification of production without meaningfully decreasing supply chain dependency on China; many recent inbound investments relocate some production without reducing dependence on China for the most valuable parts of supply chains; China has explicitly allowed geographic dispersion of production so long as control over key links in value chains remains anchored inside China. South Korea's 2026 Framework Act sets a target to cut single-country import dependence for key items below 50% by 2030.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank primary research. WebFetch verified, full content retrieved (published 23 February 2026).

title: The Global Trade Battleground: US-China Competition in the Global South
key_claim: Since 2000, Global South import shares have shifted sharply: China's share grew over 21 percentage points while the United States' fell 10 percentage points; Chinese goods exports to the Global South rose more than 39 times between 2000 and 2024 while US exports roughly doubled; by 2024 US exports to developing economies were 56% of China's.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank primary research. WebFetch verified, full content retrieved (published 6 April 2026).

title: 2026 Trade Enforcement: Why Import Compliance Is Now a Board-Level Risk
key_claim: US customs and trade enforcement is intensifying in 2026: goods determined by CBP to have been transshipped to evade duties face an additional 40% tariff with no mitigation; CBP is using AI-powered supply-chain mapping to identify transshipment and undervaluation; a DHS-DOJ Trade Task Force is pursuing False Claims Act actions for concealed transshipment; the USMCA six-year review (beginning 1 July 2026) is expected to bring tighter rules of origin and heightened scrutiny of Chinese transshipment through Mexico and Canada.
notes: Structural anchor. Tier 3 law-firm alert (per sourcing guide, a fast high-quality summary of new enforcement rules); the principal sourced basis for the counter-argument that enforcement may resolve the rerouting. WebFetch verified, full content retrieved (published 4 February 2026).
